claim: In zebrafish, arterial intersegmental vessels together with chemokines promote lymphatic cell migration from the horizontal myoseptum (HM).
source: In zebrafish, arterial intersegmental vessels together with chemokines have been shown to promote lymphatic cell migration from the horizontal myoseptum (HM).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this relationship.

claim: Emergence of mural cells around the intersegmental arteries coincides with lymphatic departure from HM.
source: We observed that emergence of mural cells around the intersegmental arteries coincides with lymphatic departure from HM which raised the possibility that arterial mural cells promote LEC migration.
evidence: This is based on observational data from live imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: LECs migrate slower in the absence of arterial mural cells.
source: Our live imaging and cell ablation experiments revealed that LECs migrate slower and fail to establish the lymphatic vascular network in the absence of arterial mural cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging and cell ablation experiments.

claim: LECs fail to establish the lymphatic vascular network in the absence of arterial mural cells.
source: Our live imaging and cell ablation experiments revealed that LECs migrate slower and fail to establish the lymphatic vascular network in the absence of arterial mural cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging and cell ablation experiments.

claim: Mural cells are a source for C-X-C motif chemokine 12 (Cxcl12a and Cxcl12b).
source: We determined that mural cells are a source for the C-X-C motif chemokine 12 (Cxcl12a and Cxcl12b), vascular endothelial growth factor C (Vegfc) and collagen and calcium-binding EGF domain-containing protein 1 (Ccbe1).
evidence: This is supported by molecular analysis including qPCR and scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mural cells are a source for vascular endothelial growth factor C (Vegfc).
source: We determined that mural cells are a source for the C-X-C motif chemokine 12 (Cxcl12a and Cxcl12b), vascular endothelial growth factor C (Vegfc) and collagen and calcium-binding EGF domain-containing protein 1 (Ccbe1).
evidence: This is supported by molecular analysis including qPCR and scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mural cells are a source for collagen and calcium-binding EGF domain-containing protein 1 (Ccbe1).
source: We determined that mural cells are a source for the C-X-C motif chemokine 12 (Cxcl12a and Cxcl12b), vascular endothelial growth factor C (Vegfc) and collagen and calcium-binding EGF domain-containing protein 1 (Ccbe1).
evidence: This is supported by molecular analysis including qPCR and scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chemokine and growth factor signalling function cooperatively to induce robust LEC migration.
source: We showed that chemokine and growth factor signalling function cooperatively to induce robust LEC migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using combinatorial inhibition approaches.

claim: Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling, but not chemokines, induces extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) activation in LECs.
source: Specifically, Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling, but not chemokines, induces extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) activation in LECs, and has an additional pro-survival role in LECs during the migration.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing pERK activation and inhibitor experiments.

claim: Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling has a pro-survival role in LECs during migration.
source: Specifically, Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling, but not chemokines, induces extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) activation in LECs, and has an additional pro-survival role in LECs during the migration.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining and cell death quantification experiments.

claim: VEGFC-mediated signalling through VEGFR3 is essential for LEC proliferation, differentiation, and migration.
source: VEGFC-mediated signalling through the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 3 (VEGFR3) is essential for multiple steps of lymphatic vessels formation, including LEC proliferation, differentiation, and migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In vitro cell culture experiments have demonstrated that VEGFC-VEGFR3 and β1 integrin promote LEC migration.
source: In vitro cell culture experiments have demonstrated that VEGFC-VEGFR3 and β1 integrin to promote LEC migration (Mäkinen et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Studies using a vegfc zebrafish reporter line have uncovered multiple sources of vegfc, including fibroblasts and neurons, which contribute to the initial sprouting and migration of lymphatic vessel into the HM.
source: Studies using a vegfc zebrafish reporter line have uncovered multiple sources of vegfc, including fibroblasts and neurons, which contribute to the initial sprouting and migration of lymphatic vessel into the HM (early migration) (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study using reporter lines.

claim: Transcription factor MAFB regulates LEC migration but not proliferation and acts downstream of VEGFC-VEGFR3 signalling.
source: Mechanistically, transcription factor MAFB, which regulates LEC migration but not proliferation, has been shown to act downstream of VEGFC-VEGFR3 signalling (Dieterich et al., 2015; Koltowska et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior mechanistic studies.

claim: A genome-wide analysis indicated the presence of a transcriptional network controlling LEC migration through the induction of chemokine receptors that promote chemotaxis in migrating LECs.
source: A genome-wide analysis further indicated the presence of a transcriptional network controlling LEC migration, through the induction of chemokine receptors that promote chemotaxis in migrating LECs (Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a genome-wide analysis study.

claim: In zebrafish trunk, lymphatic vessel specification is marked by the expression of transcription factor Prox1 in ECs around 32 hours post fertilization (hpf) in response to Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling.
source: In zebrafish trunk, lymphatic vessel specification is marked by the expression of transcription factor Prox1 in ECs around 32 hours post fertilization (hpf) in response to Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling (Koltowska et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior developmental studies in zebrafish.

claim: Around 34 hpf, venous-derived Prox1-positive cells sprout from the posterior cardinal vein (PCV) and migrate to the horizontal myoseptum (HM), establishing parachordal lymphatic endothelial cells (PLs).
source: Around 34 hpf, venous-derived Prox1-positive cells sprout from the posterior cardinal vein (PCV) and migrate to the horizontal myoseptum (HM), establishing parachordal lymphatic endothelial cells (PLs) (Hogan and Schulte-Merker, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior developmental studies.

claim: After about 10 hours the PLs move out from the HM region and migrate dorsally or ventrally, and by 5 days post fertilization (dpf) give rise to the main trunk lymphatic vessels, including dorsal longitudinal lymphatic vessel (DLLV), intersegmental lymphatic vessel (ISLV), and thoracic duct (TD).
source: After about 10 hours the PLs move out from the HM region and migrate dorsally or ventrally, and by 5 days post fertilization (dpf) give raise to the main trunk lymphatic vessels, including dorsal longitudinal lymphatic vessel (DLLV), intersegmental lymphatic vessel (ISLV), and thoracic duct (TD) (Küchler et al., 2006; Yaniv et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior developmental studies.

claim: During later migration, the vast majority of the LECs are associated with the arterial intersegmental vessels (aISVs).
source: During this later migration, the vast majority of the LECs are associated with the arterial intersegmental vessels (aISVs) (Bussmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior observational studies.

claim: PLs remain in the HM in mutant embryos lacking aISVs (plcyt26480 and kdrlhu5088 mutants).
source: Given that PLs remain in the HM, and subsequently the lymphatic network formation is compromised in mutant embryos lacking aISVs (plcyt26480 and kdrlhu5088 mutants), the aISVs are instrumental in LEC migration (Bussmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior genetic studies.

claim: Lymphatic network formation is compromised in mutant embryos lacking aISVs.
source: Given that PLs remain in the HM, and subsequently the lymphatic network formation is compromised in mutant embryos lacking aISVs (plcyt26480 and kdrlhu5088 mutants), the aISVs are instrumental in LEC migration (Bussmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior genetic studies.

claim: The aISVs are instrumental in LEC migration.
source: Given that PLs remain in the HM, and subsequently the lymphatic network formation is compromised in mutant embryos lacking aISVs (plcyt26480 and kdrlhu5088 mutants), the aISVs are instrumental in LEC migration (Bussmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and inference from genetic studies.

claim: Arterial ECs (aECs) secrete Cxcl12b to guide LEC migration via the Cxcr4 receptor expressed in LECs.
source: On the molecular level, arterial ECs (aECs) reportedly secrete Cxcl12b to guide this LECs migration via the Cxcr4 receptor expressed in LECs (Cha et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior molecular studies.

claim: Vascular mural cells (MCs) are formed de novo along aISVs and beneath the dorsal aorta simultaneous with LEC development.
source: Simultaneous with LEC development described above, vascular mural cells (MCs) are formed de novo along aISVs and beneath the dorsal aorta.
evidence: This is based on observational data and established developmental knowledge.

claim: aISVs play a critical role in MC formation, and MC emergence is completely abolished in the absence of aECs.
source: aISVs play a critical role in this process, and MC emergence is completely abolished in the absence of aECs (Ando et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior studies on MC development.

claim: MCs are sandwiched between the aISV and the migrating LEC at 4 dpf.
source: We found the spatial proximity, with MCs being sandwiched between the aISV and the migrating LEC at 4 dpf (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LECs migrated out from HM immediately after the emergence of pdgfrb+ MCs.
source: We have observed that LECs migrated out from HM immediately after the emergence of pdgfrb+ MCs (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: In approximately 90% of the cases, LEC migrated towards and interacted with the MC residing on aISV.
source: Utilizing these reporters, we found that in approximately 90% of the cases, LEC migrated towards and interacted with the MC residing on aISV (n = 21 Figure 1D–E, Figure 1—video 5, Figure 1—video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The number of MCs was not changed before and after the LEC migration.
source: The number of MCs was not changed before and after the LEC migration (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1F.

claim: LECs dynamically extended and regressed protrusions and actively reach towards the MCs when migrating out from the HM region.
source: When LECs migrated out from the HM region, we noticed that LECs dynamically extended and regressed protrusions and actively reach towards the MCs (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 4), while MCs appeared still on aISV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging observations shown in Figure 1E and supplementary videos.

claim: MCs appeared still on aISV during LEC migration.
source: When LECs migrated out from the HM region, we noticed that LECs dynamically extended and regressed protrusions and actively reach towards the MCs (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 4), while MCs appeared still on aISV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LECs in contact with the MCs migrated two times faster than LECs migrating along aISV without MCs.
source: To understand the biological significance of the interaction between LECs and MCs, we quantified the velocity of LEC migration along aISV and found that the LECs in contact with the MCs migrated two times faster than LECs migrating along aISV without MCs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative velocity measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The pdgfrbum148 mutant zebrafish showed a 30% reduction of MC number around aISVs.
source: The pdgfrbum148 mutant zebrafish (Kok et al., 2015) showed a 30% reduction of MC number around aISVs (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of MC numbers in mutants shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Trunk lymphatic vasculature formation in pdgfrbum148 mutant zebrafish revealed slight reduction in the network formation.
source: Coincidently, trunk lymphatic vasculature formation in pdgfrbum148 mutant zebrafish revealed slight reduction in the network formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: The rendering of lyve:DsRed labelled lymphatic vessels revealed on average an area of 1 mm2 in the sibling vs. 0.7 mm2 in the pdgfrbum148 mutants.
source: The rendering of lyve:DsRed labelled lymphatic vessels, as a measurement of lymphatic vessels density, revealed on average an area of 1 mm2 in the sibling vs. 0.7 mm2 in the pdgfrbum148 mutants (Figure 1H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative surface area measurements shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: Treatment with a PDGFRβ inhibitor, AG1296 from 48 hpf onwards, led to a greater reduction in MC coverage and LECs number.
source: Treatment with a PDGFRβ inhibitor, AG1296 from 48 hpf onwards, led to a greater reduction in MC coverage and LECs number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: When ablating MCs just prior to LEC migration out from HM region, LEC migration along aISV and subsequently TD formation were severely compromised.
source: When ablating MCs just prior to LEC migration out from HM region by utilizing this MC-selective NTR-MTZ ablation system, LEC migration along aISV and subsequently TD formation were severely compromised (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell ablation experiments shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: LEC migration was dramatically inhibited in the MC-ablated group compared to the control non-MC-ablated group over 5 hours post ablation.
source: The time-lapse imaging over 5 hours post ablation (hpa) confirmed that LEC migration was dramatically inhibited in the MC-ablated group compared to the control non-MC-ablated group (Figure 2F and H, Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data following laser ablation shown in Figure 2F and H.

claim: 40% of the larvae receiving MC ablation failed to form DLLV completely, while all control larvae form DLLVs.
source: We also imaged the same embryos 1 day later and observed that 40% of the larvae receiving MC ablation failed to form DLLV completely, while all control larvae form DLLVs (Figure 2G and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by follow-up imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2G and I.

claim: The absence of MCs does not affect arterial identity at early stages in zebrafish.
source: Importantly, the absence of MCs does not affect arterial identity at early stages in zebrafish (Ando et al., 2019), arguing that the importance of MC in LEC development is not simply to regulate aEC presence or abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior studies on arterial development.

claim: Even in the absence of aECs, but remaining presence of MCs, LEC migration progressed.
source: We observed that even in the absence of aECs, but remaining presence of MCs, LEC migration progressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that signals from MCs are sufficient to promote LEC migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Signals from MCs are sufficient to promote LEC migration.
source: We observed that even in the absence of aECs, but remaining presence of MCs, LEC migration progressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that signals from MCs are sufficient to promote LEC migration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that LEC migration continues without aECs but with MCs present.

claim: Two clusters express a previously identified pericyte gene signature (e.g. high levels of notch3, pdgfrb, and ndufa4l2a).
source: From this analysis we found two clusters that express a previously identified pericyte gene signature (e.g. high levels of notch3, pdgfrb, and ndufa4l2a; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as well as pericyte-like cells that lacked the definitive pericyte marker, ndufa4l2a (Shih et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pericyte-like cells lacked the definitive pericyte marker, ndufa4l2a.
source: From this analysis we found two clusters that express a previously identified pericyte gene signature (e.g. high levels of notch3, pdgfrb, and ndufa4l2a; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as well as pericyte-like cells that lacked the definitive pericyte marker, ndufa4l2a (Shih et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vegfc expression is prominent in pericyte and pericyte-like cells, with lower levels detectable in several smooth muscle cell clusters.
source: We observed prominent vegfc expression in pericyte and pericyte-like cells, with lower levels detectable in several smooth muscle cell clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq expression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only peri-like cells expressed ccbe1.
source: However, only peri-like cells expressed ccbe1.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq expression analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only a single SMC cluster expressed adamts3 while adamts14 was not detected in any clusters.
source: Similarly, only a single SMC cluster expressed adamts3 while adamts14 was not detected in any clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq expression analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cxcl12a was seen in multiple cell types with prominent expression in pericytes, as well as the two vegfc-expressing smooth muscle cell clusters.
source: Similar to vegfc, cxcl12a was seen in multiple cell types with prominent expression in pericytes, as well as the two vegfc-expressing smooth muscle cell clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq expression analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Putative pericytes expressed ackr3b, the atypical receptor for Cxcl12.
source: Interestingly, putative pericytes expressed ackr3b, the atypical receptor for Cxcl12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: LECs express ackr3b but low levels of cxcr4a and cxcr4b.
source: We observed expression of ackr3b but low levels of cxcr4a and cxcr4b (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), thus supporting previously reported expression of chemokine receptors in LECs (Cha et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis of sorted LECs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Abcc9-positive cells from dissociated trunks show significantly higher expression of cxcl12a, vegfc, and ccbe1 compared to EGFP-negative cells isolated in parallel.
source: Consistent with our scRNA-seq analysis, we found that abcc9-positive cells from dissociated trunks show significantly higher expression of cxcl12a, vegfc, and ccbe1 compared to EGFP-negative cells isolated in parallel.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis of FACS-sorted cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cxcl12a, cxcl12b, and vegfc were detected in arteries, but not ccbe1.
source: We also detected cxcl12a, cxcl12b, and vegfc in arteries, but not ccbe1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis of sorted arterial ECs shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a trend of enrichment of vegfc and ccbe1 expression in the pdgfrbhigh MCs on aISV compared to the rest of the pdgfrblow mesenchyme around aISV.
source: To confirm that vegfc and ccbe1 is expressed in the MCs, we used immunostaining of BAC-transgenic lines Tg(vegfc:Gal4; UAS:RFP; pdgfrb:GFP) and Tg(ccbe1:YFP;pdgfrb:Gal4; UAS:NTRmcherry), and observed a trend of enrichment of vegfc and ccbe1 expression in the pdgfrbhigh MCs on aISV compared to the rest of the pdgfrblow mesenchyme around aISV (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Migrating LECs are positive for phospho(p)-ERK.
source: Subsequently, we determined that migrating LECs are positive for phospho(p)-ERK (Figure 3H), which is known to be activated downstream of Vegfc-Vegfr3 or Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signalling (Spinosa et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: pERK is known to be activated downstream of Vegfc-Vegfr3 or Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signalling.
source: Subsequently, we determined that migrating LECs are positive for phospho(p)-ERK (Figure 3H), which is known to be activated downstream of Vegfc-Vegfr3 or Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signalling (Spinosa et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior signaling studies.

claim: Chemokines have been shown to be important for LEC migration with LECs being attracted by mosaic overexpression of cxcl12b.
source: Chemokines have been shown to be important for LEC migration with LECs being attracted by mosaic overexpression of cxcl12b, whereas the cxcl12a, cxcl12b, and cxcr4a mutants show defects in TD formation (Cha et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior studies on chemokine function.

claim: The cxcl12a, cxcl12b, and cxcr4a mutants show defects in TD formation.
source: Chemokines have been shown to be important for LEC migration with LECs being attracted by mosaic overexpression of cxcl12b, whereas the cxcl12a, cxcl12b, and cxcr4a mutants show defects in TD formation (Cha et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior genetic studies.

claim: In AMD3100-treated embryos, LECs migrated shorter distances with decreased velocity compared with the controls.
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed that in AMD3100-treated embryos, LECs migrated shorter distances with decreased velocity compared with the controls (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: An increased number of filopodia was found in AMD3100-treated embryos reaching statistical significance 7.5 hours after exposure.
source: We found an increased number of filopodia reaching statistical significance 7.5 hours after exposure (Figure 4E–F, Figure 4—videos 5–8).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of filopodia formation shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Filopodia formation extended not only towards the migrating front but also laterally in AMD3100-treated embryos, implying the compromised directional migration of LECs.
source: We observed filopodia formation extended not only towards the migrating front but also laterally in AMD3100-treated embryos, implying the compromised directional migration of LECs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of filopodia orientation in treated embryos.

claim: LEC apoptosis was not observed in the AMD3100-treated embryos.
source: While, we did not observe the LEC apoptosis in the AMD3100-treated embryos.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the experiments.

claim: Tracing the migration distance revealed a reduced number of migrating cells and increased number of cells that stalled or regressed their migration in SL327-treated embryos.
source: Tracing the migration distance revealed a reduced number of migrating cells and increased number of cells that stalled or regressed their migration in SL327-treated embryos (n = 5) (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: A dramatic decrease of LEC division from 25% in controls to 1.5% in SL327-treated embryos was found.
source: In addition, we found a dramatic decrease of LEC division from 25% in controls to 1.5% in SL327-treated embryos (Figure 4J–K), which is in agreement with the known necessary role of Vegfc-Vegfr3 in cell proliferation (Cao et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of cell division shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: Vegfc-Vegfr3 has a known necessary role in cell proliferation.
source: In addition, we found a dramatic decrease of LEC division from 25% in controls to 1.5% in SL327-treated embryos (Figure 4J–K), which is in agreement with the known necessary role of Vegfc-Vegfr3 in cell proliferation (Cao et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior studies on Vegfc-Vegfr3 signaling.

claim: SL327 treatment induced cell death in 7 out of 12 cells.
source: SL327 treatment induced cell death in 7 out of 12 cells, which was further confirmed by TUNEL staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C), suggesting that during this lymphatic developmental window ERK activation acts as a LEC pro-survival factor.
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: During this lymphatic developmental window ERK activation acts as a LEC pro-survival factor.
source: SL327 treatment induced cell death in 7 out of 12 cells, which was further confirmed by TUNEL staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C), suggesting that during this lymphatic developmental window ERK activation acts as a LEC pro-survival factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ERK inhibition leads to cell death.

claim: ERK activation is primarily induced by Vegfc during the LEC specification and sprouting from the PCV.
source: It has been reported that ERK activation is primarily induced by Vegfc during the LEC specification and sprouting from the PCV (Karkkainen et al., 2004; Koltowska et al., 2015a), our results showed that Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling also instructs LEC in the subsequent migratory events from HM to establish the lymphatic vessel network in the trunk.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on ERK activation.

claim: Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling instructs LEC in the subsequent migratory events from HM to establish the lymphatic vessel network in the trunk.
source: It has been reported that ERK activation is primarily induced by Vegfc during the LEC specification and sprouting from the PCV (Karkkainen et al., 2004; Koltowska et al., 2015a), our results showed that Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling also instructs LEC in the subsequent migratory events from HM to establish the lymphatic vessel network in the trunk.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing ERK activation and migration defects.

claim: Embryos treated with soluble Flt4 showed severe impairments in LEC migration.
source: Embryos treated with soluble Flt4 showed severe impairments in LEC migration (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: No difference in LEC survival was observed between heatshock only and the combinatory-treated group.
source: In addition, we observed no difference in LEC survival between in heatshock only and the combinatory-treated group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The combinatory treatment further decreased the LEC migrating distance, but only marginally.
source: The combinatory treatment further decreased the LEC migrating distance, but only marginally.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of migration distance in combinatorial treatment experiments.

claim: No additive effects on the velocity of migrating LEC were observed by the combinatory treatment, suggesting cooperation rather than mechanistic interaction of these two signalling pathways in the coordination of LEC migration.
source: Interestingly we observed no additive effects on the velocity of migrating LEC by the combinatory treatment, suggesting cooperation rather than mechanistic interaction of these two signalling pathways in the coordination of LEC migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effects in combinatorial inhibition experiments.

claim: A dramatic reduction in LEC numbers and ERK activation was observed upon soluble Flt4 treatment or combinatory treatment but not in AMD3100-treated group.
source: As expected, we observed a dramatic reduction in LEC numbers and ERK activation upon soluble Flt4 treatment or combinatory treatment but not in AMD3100-treated group (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: No change in ERK activation was observed in AMD3100 treatment alone.
source: Surprisingly, we overserved no change in ERK activation in AMD3100 treatment alone (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ERK activation may be induced mainly via Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling rather than Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signalling during LEC migration.
source: Thus, these data indicate that ERK activation may be induced mainly via Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling rather than Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signalling during LEC migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Vegfr3 and Cxcr4 inhibition on ERK activation.

claim: Chemokine and Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling pathways cooperate to promote proper LEC migration.
source: Together, our data provide evidence that these signalling pathways cooperate to promote proper LEC migration (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is inferred from the combinatorial inhibition experiments showing cooperation.

claim: MCs provide a signalling threshold for LECs to robustly migrate from the HM region and progress dorsally across the trunk of the embryo.
source: We speculate that MCs provided a signalling threshold for LECs robustly migrate from the HM region and progress dorsally across the trunk of the embryo.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Multiple cellular sources work together to establish the favourable levels of signalling for LEC migration.
source: Based on observations from Wang et al. and Karpanen et al., which uncovered cellular constituents for lymphangiogenic factors at earlier stages of LEC development (Karpanen et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020) and our study revealing role for MC in LEC migration, thus it becomes evident that multiple cellular sources work together to establish the favourable levels of signalling for LEC migration.
evidence: This is inferred from integration of current findings with prior studies.

claim: Chemokines are necessary for the progression of LEC migration and in their absence migrating cells show an increased number of filopodia, suggesting a loss in directionality.
source: We have determined that chemokines are necessary for the progression of LEC migration and in their absence migrating cells show an increased number of filopodia, suggesting a loss in directionality.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from AMD3100 treatment experiments.

claim: Inhibition of Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling leads to more severe phenotypes where disrupted LEC migration was accompanied by reduced proliferation and increased cell death.
source: Whereas inhibition of Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling lead to more severe phenotypes where disrupted LEC migration was accompanied by reduced proliferation and increased cell death.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from soluble Flt4 and SL327 treatment experiments.

claim: During the LEC migration Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling has a dual role in guiding lymphatic and promoting their survival.
source: This uncovers that during the LEC migration Vegfc-Vegfr3 signalling has a dual role in guiding lymphatic and promoting their survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both migration and survival defects upon Vegfc-Vegfr3 inhibition.

claim: The published migratory phenotypes in the cxcl12a, cxcl12b, and cxcr4a mutants are milder to the ones observed in the SL327 drug treatment experiment or the cell ablation experiments.
source: It is important to note that the published migratory phenotypes in the cxcl12a, cxcl12b, and cxcr4a mutants are milder (Cha et al., 2012) to the ones observed in the SL327 drug treatment experiment or the cell ablation experiments.
evidence: This is based on comparison of current experimental results with published mutant phenotypes.

claim: Additional chemokine receptors might act together to regulate LEC migration.
source: Thus, additional chemokine receptors might act together to regulate LEC migration.
evidence: This is speculated based on the discrepancy between mutant and inhibitor phenotypes.

claim: Higher levels of atypical receptor ackr3b (cxcr7) than cxcr4 were observed in LECs.
